sections.title: The First Converts
sections.html:
The first of the converts was Avraham our father, who was born into a family of idol worshipers, and out of his good character traits and deep contemplation came to know his Creator and denied the idols of his father's house. When he was about fifty-two years old he began to spread faith in the One God, and together with Sara our mother he converted men and women to the service of God (Avoda Zara 9a; above 1:9). At the age of seventy-five he merited a Divine revelation, and was commanded to go up to the land and to found in it a nation from which blessing would spread to all the families of the earth (Bereishit 12:1-3).

The life of Avraham our father is an example and model for all converts. Like Avraham, they too leave the land of their birth and their family, their faith and their culture, join the people of Israel and go up to the land in order to participate in realizing the great vision of Israel – to bring blessing to the whole world. This is what is stated (Tehillim 47:10): "The nobles of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Avraham." The converts are the "nobles of the peoples" who gather by their own choice to the destiny of the children of Avraham, "who was the first of the converts" (Sukka 49b).

When Pharaoh king of Egypt decreed that the children of Israel be cast into the Nile, Yokheved hid her three-month-old baby son in an ark among the reeds by the Nile, in order to save him from the Egyptians who sought to kill all the sons born to Israel. "And Pharaoh's daughter went down to bathe at the Nile, and her maidens walked along the Nile's edge; and she saw the ark among the reeds and sent her maidservant, and she took it. And she opened it and saw the child, and behold, a boy crying; and she had compassion on him and said: This is one of the Hebrews' children … And he became her son, and she called his name Moshe, and she said: Because I drew him out of the water" (Shemot 2:1-10). At that very time, when Bitya daughter of Pharaoh decided to defy her father's decree and save the Hebrew child, Bitya denied the idols of her father's house and joined the people of Israel, and her bathing in the Nile served for her as the immersion of conversion (Megilla 13a; Rashi, ibid.).

When Israel left Egypt, Bitya joined them, and married Kalev son of Yefuneh, who was called 'Mered,' because he rebelled (marad) against and repudiated the counsel of the spies, and walked in the way of his wife Bitya, who had rebelled against her father's command to murder the children of Israel. And Bitya was called 'the Jewess' (ha-Yehudiya) "because she repudiated idolatry," "for whoever repudiates idolatry is called a Jew" (Megilla, ibid.). Concerning Bitya daughter of Pharaoh the verse is stated (I Divrei Ha-yamim 4:18): "And his wife the Jewess bore Yered the father of Gedor, and Ḥever the father of Sokho, and Yekutiel the father of Zanoaḥ; and these are the sons of Bitya the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took." The Sages said (Megilla, ibid.) that all the names mentioned as sons whom Bitya bore are nothing but epithets of Moshe our teacher, whom she merited to save and raise, "to tell you that whoever raises an orphan boy or girl in his home, Scripture regards him as though he had given birth to him … And why was he called Yered? Because manna descended (yarad) for Israel in his days. Gedor – because he fenced in (gadar) the breaches of Israel. Ḥever – because he connected (ḥiber) Israel to their Father in Heaven. Sokho – because he became for Israel like a sukka (a shelter). Yekutiel – because Israel hoped (kivu) to God in his days. Zanoaḥ – because he caused the sins of Israel to be disregarded (hiznia'ḥ) (he caused God to forgive Israel for their sins). 'Father of,' 'father of,' 'father of' – a father in Torah, a father in wisdom, a father in prophecy."

sections.title: Yitro
sections.html:
All his days Yitro searched for the purpose of man and the secret of life. To this end he studied all the idolatrous religions that existed in his time and strove to worship all the idols (Mekhilta on Shemot 18:11). In time he became the chief priest in Midyan, and his name became so famous that he was called to serve as a priest and adviser to Pharaoh, king of the Egyptian empire. When the harsh decrees against Israel began, he began to have misgivings, and when they reached the decree "Every son that is born you shall cast into the Nile" (Shemot 1:22), his conscience rebelled. He tried to annul the decree, and when he did not succeed he fled to Midyan and returned to being their priest (see Shemot Rabba 27:6; Sota 11a). But after all the wickedness he had seen in Egypt, done under the auspices of the idols, his heart smote him and he could no longer continue to believe in idols. "He called the people of his city and said to them: Until now I have served you; from now on, since I am old, choose another priest for yourselves. He took out his implements of idolatrous worship and gave them to them." The Midianites understood that he had begun to repudiate idolatry; they rose up and ostracized him, and decreed that no one should help him with his work or tend his flock, until he was forced to ask his daughters to tend his flock (Shemot Rabba 1:32), and the shepherds would harass his daughters and deprive them of their turn to water the flock. Meanwhile Moshe, who had fled from Pharaoh, arrived and sat by the well. When he saw the shepherds depriving Yitro's daughters, he stood up for them and watered their flock. Following this he married Tzippora daughter of Yitro and began to tend Yitro's flock.

After some years God revealed Himself to Moshe and sent him to save Israel from Egypt. Yitro had already despaired of his aspiration to arrive at the truth and to repair the world, and therefore he greatly feared for the life of Moshe, who was going to stand up against the wicked kingdom. But when he heard that God had saved Israel from Egypt through Moshe his son-in-law, the deep desire to know his purpose and to draw close to God was reawakened in his heart. Although it was not easy for a wise and experienced old man like him to begin learning a new religion, his yearning for true faith prevailed, and he sought to join Israel. But he feared that, being a foreigner, they would push him away and belittle his wisdom and his life experience. And even though Moshe was his son-in-law, and in Moshe's time of distress he had helped him, he feared that after becoming a leader Moshe might estrange himself from his wife and his father-in-law, as is the way of many people who rise to greatness and disown their past. Out of these fears he approached the camp of Israel and sent word to Moshe: Please, come out toward me to receive me with a pleasant countenance, for I am your father-in-law. And if not for my honor, then at least come out toward your wife who has come with me, or at least toward your sons who are coming with us. Moshe our teacher, too, was apprehensive, lest Yitro wished to benefit from his honor and glory, and would turn the hearts of Israel to the idolatry to which he had been accustomed.

God revealed Himself to Moshe and said to him: "This man who comes to Me comes only for the sake of Heaven, and comes only to convert. You too, draw him near; do not push him away." Moshe understood that it was fitting to honor Yitro, and went out toward him with honor. Since this was so, Aharon his brother and his sons Nadav and Avihu, and the seventy elders, joined him, and with them many of Israel. And some say that the Ark of the Covenant also went out with them (Mekhilta). When they reached Yitro, Moshe our teacher bowed to him, kissed him, asked after his welfare, brought him into his tent, and told him all the kindnesses that God had done for Israel in the Exodus from Egypt (Shemot 18:7; Mekhilta; Shemot Rabba 27:2). Thus all of Israel learned how one must receive the righteous converts with honor and love.

Through this they merited the good advice that Yitro gave Moshe our teacher and Israel concerning the order of administering justice. Because of the great importance of his words, they were even set down in the Torah, and it became clear that the word of God was in his mouth. Not only that, but the Sages said that Yitro merited that from then until today there has not been a generation in which the study halls lacked his descendants; from them came forth great Torah scholars and people endowed with divine inspiration, and some of them sat in the Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and all of Israel heard halakha from their mouths (Sota 11a; Tanḥuma, Vayakhel 8; Tanna De-Vei Eliyahu Rabba 6).

sections.title: The Difficulties and the Success
sections.html:
Although Yitro, Moshe's father-in-law, was one of the greatest converts, difficulties accompanied his conversion too, for it is impossible that such a deep process of taking root in a new people with a sanctified heritage should pass without friction and hurt feelings. And so the Torah relates (Bemidbar 10:29-32) that when Israel began to travel to the Land of Israel, Moshe our teacher said to Yitro: "We are traveling to the place of which the Lord said, 'I will give it to you'; come with us and we will do you good, for the Lord has spoken good concerning Israel." But Yitro replied: "I will not go; rather, to my land and to my birthplace I will go." The Sages explained that Yitro feared that he would have no place among Moshe and Aharon and all the sages of Israel, and would feel superfluous; therefore he preferred to return to Midyan, to spread the word of God there and to convert the members of his family and his city (Sifrei Zuta). And some say that Yitro understood that the Land of Israel would be divided among the Children of Israel who had been enslaved in Egypt, and if so, he and his descendants would have no inheritance in the land and would have to live in disgrace (Rashi). But Moshe our teacher urged him to remain with them and to continue contributing to Israel from his wisdom and his guidance, as it is stated: "And he said: Please do not leave us, for you know how we are to encamp in the wilderness, and you shall be as eyes for us." Against the concern that he and his sons would have no place in the land, Moshe promised that Israel would do him good from the goodness of the Land of Israel, as it is stated: "And it shall be, if you go with us, that whatever good the Lord does for us, we will do for you." Granted, he could not promise Yitro a permanent inheritance in the land, but he could commit that the Children of Israel would do good to Yitro's sons from the goodness of the land. When Israel conquered the land, and Yeriḥo, which was a fertile oasis, they consecrated Yeriḥo as the place from which they would supply food for the Temple. And they established that until the Temple was built, Yitro's sons would live in Yeriḥo in tents, and their dwelling there continued for four hundred and forty years (Rashi and Radak on Shofetim 1:16).

And some of the sons of Yitro – one of whose epithets was 'Keini' – spread out on the edge of the wilderness, on the fringes of the settled areas, in territories that had not been apportioned to the families of Israel, and their status was complex. They were at peace with Yavin king of Canaan, who subjugated Israel, so much so that Sisera his army commander thought to find refuge with them. But when he reached the tent of Yael, the wife of Ḥever the Keinite, she revealed her loyalty to Israel, and after lulling him to sleep she killed him with a tent peg, thereby bringing a great salvation to Israel (Shofetim 4:17-22). Since the Keinites lived as neighbors of the Amalekites, when Shaul came to strike Amalek he needed to warn the descendants of Yitro to move away from among the Amalekites so that they would not be harmed in the battles (I Shmuel 15:6). Apparently, throughout all those years many of Yitro's descendants took root in the tribes of Israel.

After the Temple was built, some of the Keinites who remained in Yeriḥo joined their brethren who had already taken root in Israel. But there remained a core of Yitro's descendants who continued to be called 'Keinites,' or 'the sons of Rekhav' after the father of their family, and they continued to live in tents on the edge of the wilderness, content with little and cleaving to God. When, at the command of Elisha the prophet, Yehu the army commander rebelled against the dynasty of Aḥav and set out to destroy the worship of Ba'al from Israel, he sought the help of Yehonadav son of Rekhav and took him into his chariot (II Melakhim 10:15-16). About two hundred years later, when Yirmeyahu the prophet prophesied about the destruction and rebuked Israel for not cleaving to the ways of God, he cited as an example the sons of Rekhav, who kept the command of their father, abstained from wine, and did not live in houses but in tents, so that they would always remember God and live many days on the land (Yirmeyahu 35). Through this the sons of Rekhav merited to pass through the destruction with less suffering and loss, and merited to produce Torah scholars for generation after generation (Sifrei Zuta, ibid.; Mekhilta De-Rashbi, Shemot 18; Rashi).1

sections.title: Raḥav
sections.html:
When Israel were about to enter the Land of Israel and conquer it, Yehoshua son of Nun sent two spies to Yeriḥo to examine the situation of the Canaanites. The Sages said that these spies were among the greatest of Israel – Kalev son of Yefuneh and Pinḥas son of Elazar son of Aharon the Kohen. They came to the inn of Raḥav the harlot in Yeriḥo, but word of their arrival reached the king of Yeriḥo, who sent to order Raḥav to hand them over. But following the reports of the Exodus from Egypt, the splitting of the Sea of Reeds and the victories over Siḥon and Og, the kings of the Emori, a great fear had fallen upon Raḥav, and she had begun to believe in the Lord God of Israel as mightier than all; therefore she hid the spies on the roof and told the king's messengers that they had already gone and left the city. After the king's messengers left, she went up to them on the roof and said that she knew that Israel would conquer the land, "for the Lord your God, He is God in heaven above and on the earth below." As a result, she asked them to swear to her by the Lord that when they conquered Yeriḥo they would save and keep alive all the members of her family. They set a sign: when they conquered Yeriḥo, Raḥav would tie a cord of crimson (red) thread from the window of her house in the wall, through which she had helped them escape from the city, and by it Israel would know where her house was and would save all the members of her family who were with her in the house (Yehoshua 2; Zevaḥim 116a).

The Sages said that all the years that Israel were studying Torah in the wilderness, Raḥav was a harlot with princes and robbers (Zevaḥim 116b). Apparently she had a soul that lusted for life, and therefore she tried to taste and experience everything. But however much she searched and tried, she felt unsatisfied. When Israel drew near to the land, she understood that the Lord God of Israel is the One who rules over everything and He is the source of life, and that in all her searching she had always wanted to draw close to Him. And even though the Canaanites still ruled the land, she had the courage to ask to join Israel and to convert.

From Raḥav the harlot we learn that even one who was sunk in lusts and sinned much can believe in God, repent and rise without limit. Not only that, but the Sages praised the excellence of her faith, for she had the insight to understand that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth below, which is the essence of the faith in God's unity that is revealed in heavenly truth and in the joy of life on earth (see Devarim Rabba 2:28). The Sages said that after she converted, Yehoshua son of Nun married her, and they merited that from their daughters came eight Kohanim who were also prophets: Neriya, Barukh, Seraya, Maḥseya, Yirmeya, Ḥilkiya, Ḥanamel and Shalum; and some say also Ḥulda the prophetess (Megilla 14b), and Yeḥezkel the prophet (Pesikta De-Rav Kahana 13). The Sages said (Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:8): "When Israel do the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, He searches throughout the entire world and sees which righteous person there is among the nations of the world, and brings him and attaches him to Israel, such as Yitro and Raḥav."

sections.title: Rut
sections.html:
The story of Rut the convert is one of the foundational stories about converts. At one of the low points of the period of the Judges, when a severe famine struck the land, Elimelekh and his family went down from Beit Leḥem in Judea to the land of Moav. Elimelekh and his wife Naomi were among the most important descendants of a wealthy and distinguished family of the tribe of Yehuda, from which, according to the testament of Yaakov our father to his sons, the king of Israel was destined to arise. But following the crises and difficulties of the period of the Judges, Elimelekh despaired of Israel's future, and when famine visited the land, he turned his back on the poor of his people and, in order to save his property, went down with his family to the land of Moav. Elimelekh and his family began their new life in Moav, but blessing departed from them. Within ten years Elimelekh died. His sons, Maḥlon and Kilyon, married Rut and Orpa, who were connected by lineage to the royal family of Moav, and tried to continue his business, but they became impoverished and died. Naomi, who was left a bereaved and poor widow, heard that the famine in the Land of Israel had ended and decided to return to her abandoned home in Beit Leḥem. Out of respect for their deceased husbands and out of their love for Naomi, her widowed daughters-in-law asked to accompany her. Naomi hugged them and kissed them, but out of responsibility for their future, she urged them to return to their parents' homes, to marry and to raise families. Her daughters-in-law raised their voices and wept, and asked to go with her. Naomi explained to them that if they went with her they would remain lonely widows until the day of their death, for there was no chance that they would find a husband in Israel. And it seems they would also not be received sympathetically, since their husbands, her sons, were regarded as traitors to Yehuda, who had abandoned their own people in days of famine. In Moav, by contrast, capable women like them would merit to marry and raise families. Orpa kissed Naomi and returned home, but Rut clung to her mother-in-law. Naomi said to Rut: Behold, your sister-in-law has returned to her people; you too return and build yourself a family. "And Rut said: Do not entreat me to leave you, to turn back from following you; for wherever you go I will go, and wherever you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried; thus may the Lord do to me, and more also, if anything but death parts me from you" (Rut 1:16-17). Out of a moral obligation to the memory of her dead husband, and out of a desire to stand by her poor mother-in-law, so that she would not remain bereaved and lonely to the end of her life, Rut's heart opened to faith in the Lord God of Israel, and she decided to convert and to join Israel in an eternal covenant, even if she would be forced to remain lonely and poor until the day of her death.

Apparently, out of great shame Naomi wanted to return to her home in Beit Leḥem secretly, from behind the city, along the road leading to the cemetery. But just then the funeral of the wife of Boaz, the greatest man of the generation, was taking place (Bava Batra 91a). And so it came about that all the participants in the funeral passed by Naomi as she returned defeated to her abandoned home. They remembered her wealth and lineage, how she used to go out in the splendor of chariots and in magnificent clothes, and now her clothes were worn out, her face gaunt with hunger, and a young foreign woman was with her (Rut Rabba 3:6). "And the whole city was astir over them, and the women said: Is this Naomi?!" "And she said to them: Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the Lord has brought me back empty; why do you call me Naomi, when the Lord has testified against me and the Almighty has afflicted me?"

Naomi and Rut were hungry for bread, but they preserved their dignity and refrained from going from door to door to the wealthy to ask for charity. Those were the days of the beginning of the barley harvest, and the Torah established a mitzva to leave for the poor leket (gleanings), shikheḥa (forgotten sheaves) and pe'a (the corner of the field); but going out for this together with all the poor was a terrible humiliation for Naomi. Rut the Moabite volunteered to go out in a foreign land to glean the gifts for the poor for them. By chance she came to the field of Boaz. The young men talked about her, and Boaz, who noticed her modesty and her goodness of heart, feared that some would mistreat her and exploit her weakness. To protect her, he asked her to keep coming to glean in his field, and at the same time ordered his young men to honor her with some of their food and to leave a great deal of barley for her. When Rut returned to Naomi, she told her that a certain man, Boaz, had honored her and treated her kindly. Naomi understood that perhaps their redemption would come from him, for although Boaz was many years older than Rut, he was her relative, and if he agreed to marry Rut in a kind of levirate marriage (yibum), they could have a child through whom her family would be restored. In her wisdom Naomi devised a plan in which Rut would express, in the deepest and most courageous way, her desire to marry Boaz despite his being older than she. But they had a twofold problem: first, there was a halakhic doubt whether it was permitted to marry a Moabite convert. Second, there was another man more closely related to Elimelekh than Boaz, and he had the first right to take Rut in levirate marriage. After it was ruled that it was permitted to marry her, and that relative refused to take her in levirate marriage, Boaz married her. "So Boaz took Rut, and she became his wife, and he came to her, and the Lord gave her conception, and she bore a son. And the women said to Naomi: Blessed is the Lord, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be famous in Israel. And he shall be to you a restorer of life and a sustainer of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you has borne him, she who is better to you than seven sons. And Naomi took the child and laid him in her bosom, and became his nurse." In her great generosity Rut included Naomi in raising the child, to the point that the neighbors said, "A son has been born to Naomi."

Thus Rut, through her great kindness and devotion, redeemed all those around her. By her merit the sin of Elimelekh, Maḥlon and Kilyon, who went down to Moav, was turned to the good, and Naomi, who had not protested against them, merited to be comforted by a child who grew up on her knees. Boaz too was redeemed, for he had had thirty sons and all of them died in his lifetime (Bava Batra 91a), and by virtue of Rut he merited a son who continued his heritage.

Many years passed, Boaz and Naomi passed away, and God showed kindness to Rut and lengthened her days greatly, and she merited to see David, her great-grandson, save Israel and found in Jerusalem his royal dynasty for all generations. She even merited to see Shlomo sitting on his royal throne, and they would call her 'the mother of royalty,' and on festive occasions they would seat her on an honored chair beside King Shlomo. And everyone knew that the royal family in Israel arose by virtue of the great kindness of the great-grandmother, this righteous convert (I Melakhim 2:19; Bava Batra 91b).2

sections.title: Shemaya and Avtalyon
sections.html:
The contribution of righteous converts to the revelation of the Oral Torah was immense, to the point that one cannot describe the chain of transmission of the Oral Torah without them. To a certain extent they have an advantage: since they came from outside and the power of choice is prominent in them, they can innovate more in their learning (above 1:6, note 3). Many times it was specifically from the descendants of the wicked among the nations of the world that holy souls were roused to draw close to Israel and convert. Apparently they had great powers. When they did not merit, they were exceedingly wicked; and when their descendants merited to repent and convert, they merited to rectify the sins of their forefathers and to add great blessing to Israel and the world.

Among the greatest of the converts were Shemaya and Avtalyon, descendants of Sanḥeriv, king of the Assyrian empire, who brought destruction upon the cities of Judea and sought to destroy Jerusalem (Gittin 57b). Shemaya and Avtalyon led the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem in the days of Queen Shlomtzion and her sons. Shemaya was the Nasi (president) of the Sanhedrin and Avtalyon was the Av Beit Din (head of the court) (see below 9, note 12).

The Sages said: There was an incident with a High Priest who came out in peace from the Yom Kippur service in the Holy of Holies, and as was the accepted custom, the multitudes of the House of Israel followed him to accompany him to his home. When they saw Shemaya and Avtalyon coming to bless the High Priest, they turned away from him toward Shemaya and Avtalyon to pay them honor. The High Priest was offended by this, and when Shemaya and Avtalyon reached him to bless him, he sought to humiliate them and remind them of their lowly origin, and said: "Let the descendants of the nations come in peace." And they in their wisdom answered him: "Worthy of the blessing of peace are the descendants of the nations who act according to the way of Aharon the Kohen, who pursued peace, and not the descendant of Aharon who does not act according to the way of Aharon" (Yoma 71b). One of their great disciples was Hillel, who learned from them the essence of his teaching, and he used to say: "Be among the disciples of Aharon – loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah" (Avot 1:12).

sections.title: Onkelos the Convert
sections.html:
There was a wonderful righteous convert in the generation after the destruction of the Second Temple: Onkelos, the son of the sister of the emperor of Rome, which destroyed the Temple. Onkelos merited to go up to the Land of Israel and to study with two of the greatest Tanna'im: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

The Sages said that when Onkelos was deliberating whether to convert, he raised by necromancy Titus, the emperor of Rome who destroyed the Temple, and Bil'am the wicked, who wanted to curse Israel, and asked them whether it was worthwhile for him to convert. They advised him not to convert, because they held that he would not succeed in fulfilling the many mitzvot of Israel. And even though they admitted that they were being punished in Gehinnom for their persecution of Israel, they recommended that he persecute Israel so that he would at least succeed in this world. But when he raised by necromancy 'that man,' he replied that it was worthwhile for him to convert (Gittin 56b-57a). The Sages further related that when he was about to convert, he feared that his act would arouse anger in the emperor's house. To prevent this he went to his uncle the emperor, told him that he wished to engage in commerce, and asked his advice. The emperor suggested that he buy merchandise that was lowly and cheap but destined to rise in price, and he would make a large profit from its sale. He went to the Land of Israel, studied Torah and converted without the emperor's knowledge. Later the emperor met him and saw that his face had changed. He asked: Have you lost your money, or perhaps someone persecuted you? Onkelos answered him that he had converted and undergone circumcision, and he was still weak from it. The emperor protested: Who suggested that you do this?! He replied: I consulted you and did as you advised, for the Jewish people is at a low point and is destined to rise and be redeemed. Nevertheless the emperor was angry with him, but did not want to kill him because he was his relative (Tanḥuma, Mishpatim 5).3

As we have learned (above 1:3), even when a great person comes to convert, because of the gaps in language and culture it is almost impossible for his absorption to pass without hurt feelings, and therefore the Torah strongly warned to safeguard the honor of the convert. It is related that Onkelos asked Rabbi Eliezer: Why is it stated that God "loves the stranger, giving him bread and clothing" (Devarim 10:18)? I am accustomed to eating fowl, quail and choice foods, and even my servants eat of them; why then does God promise to give the convert the paltry reward of bread and clothing?! Rabbi Eliezer answered him that it is not right to belittle bread and clothing, for there are poor people who do not have even bread and clothing; and even Yaakov our father pleaded with God to give him bread and garments, whereas to the convert God promised bread and clothing without pleading. Rabbi Eliezer's disciples sensed that Onkelos had been hurt by the answer, and referred him to Rabbi Yehoshua, who appeased him with words, and explained to him that 'bread' alludes to the Torah and to the showbread, and 'clothing' alludes to the tallit and to the priestly garments, for the daughter of a convert may marry a Kohen, and thus the convert's grandson can be a High Priest and wear the magnificent priestly garments. "They said: Were it not for the patience that Rabbi Yehoshua showed Onkelos, he would have returned to his former ways," and concerning this it is stated (Mishlei 16:32): "Better is one who is slow to anger than a mighty man" (Bereishit Rabba 70:5; Kohelet Rabba 7:8). By virtue of Rabbi Yehoshua's patience, Onkelos continued to study with him and with Rabbi Eliezer, and rose in Torah until he bestowed his translation upon the people of Israel.

Onkelos represents the converts who grew up in wealthy kingdoms and understood with the depth of their minds that their culture was heading toward decline, and understood the great tidings hidden in the Torah of Israel, through which the redemption will come.4

During those generations most of the people of Israel spoke Aramaic, and therefore there was a great need to translate the Torah into Aramaic for them. Granted, Ezra the Scribe had already translated the Torah into Aramaic, but the tradition of his translation became corrupted and forgotten, and there was a need to write the translation anew; and this great work was done by Onkelos (Megilla 3a). The work of translation is very difficult, for if the translation is only literal, there will be many distortions in it. Therefore Onkelos needed to delve very deeply into understanding the content of the Torah as it was transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, and to cast its content into an accurate and concise translation (see Kiddushin 49a, Rashi). His teachers, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, were also greatly impressed by his translation, praised it and said: "You are fairer than the children of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever" (Tehillim 45:3; Yerushalmi Megilla 1:9).

Because of the great stature of Targum Onkelos, the Sages instituted that all of Israel should read the weekly Torah portion every week 'twice the Scripture and once the Targum' (Berakhot 8a; Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:9-10). And even though there came generations in which many of Israel did not speak Aramaic, they continued to encourage its reading, for its foundation is from Sinai and it was written with divine inspiration. The Kabbalists further explained that through reading Targum Onkelos one elevates from the profane (from the kelipat noga) that which can be sanctified. For the Targum complements the holy tongue and sifts out of the profane all the sparks that are fit to rise and join the holy (see Likutei Moharan 19:4-6).

sections.title: Rabbi Akiva, Son of Converts
sections.html:
Rabbi Akiva, too, who studied Torah with tremendous devotion until he became the greatest of the sages of the Oral Torah, was the son of converts. He was born to Yosef the convert, and at first he was an am ha-aretz (an unlearned man), and only at the age of forty did he begin to study Torah. Rabbi Akiva related about himself that during the forty years that he was an am ha-aretz, he hated Torah scholars and would say: "Would that I had a Torah scholar, and I would bite him like a donkey" (Pesaḥim 49b). It is possible that his father did not convert in the ideal manner, and therefore he raised his son as an am ha-aretz who hated sages; and perhaps he converted properly for the sake of Heaven, but because of the difficulties of absorption he did not succeed in educating his son to love the Torah and those who study it. The Sages further said that Rabbi Akiva was a descendant of Sisera, the army commander who fought against Israel in the days of Devora the prophetess (Gittin 57b).5

Rabbi Akiva's starting conditions were exceedingly poor, but there was a good root in him, and Raḥel, the daughter of 'Kalba Savua,' one of the wealthiest men of Jerusalem, discerned his virtue and agreed to marry him if he would devote himself to Torah study. Her wealthy father opposed her choice and forbade her by vow from benefiting from any of his property. But she did not budge from her position; she married Rabbi Akiva and became the poorest and lowliest woman in Israel, and continued with wondrous self-sacrifice to encourage her husband to study Torah diligently. Therefore, when Rabbi Akiva became the greatest of his generation, he said to his students: "What is mine and what is yours – is hers" (Ketubot 63a).

"Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: When Moshe ascended on high, he found the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and tying crowns to the letters. He said before Him: Master of the Universe, who is holding You back? (Who requires the precision of these crowns? Surely there is no one who understands their meaning!) He said to him: There is one man who will be at the end of several generations, and Akiva son of Yosef is his name, who is destined to expound upon each and every thorn heaps upon heaps of halakhot … He said before Him: Master of the Universe, You have such a man, and You give the Torah through me?! He said to him: Be silent; so it arose in thought before Me" (Menaḥot 29b). From the fact that of all the sages of Israel the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moshe our teacher specifically Rabbi Akiva, it is implied that he was regarded as the greatest of the Oral Torah. The Sages likewise said that the Mishna, the Tosefta and the halakhic Midrashim were taught by the students of Rabbi Akiva, and all the anonymous halakhot of the Sages, stated without mention of who said them, derive from Rabbi Akiva (Sanhedrin 86a; below 9:9).

Rabbi Akiva's contribution to the people of Israel was especially important. He lived in the generation after the destruction of the Second Temple, in the days of the Roman persecutions against Israel up to the Bar Kokhba revolt. Through the greatness of his faith he breathed a spirit of faith into Israel, so that even when he saw a fox coming out of the ruins of the Holy of Holies, and his colleagues wept in grief over the destruction, he learned from this that just as all the prophecies of calamity in the Prophets were fulfilled, so too all the prophecies of consolation will be fulfilled; and thus he succeeded in comforting his colleagues and gladdening them (see Makkot 24b). Through the depth of his learning he breathed tremendous vitality into Torah study. Through his emphasis on the value of the mitzvot between man and his fellow, saying: "'You shall love your fellow as yourself' – this is a great principle of the Torah" (Vayikra 19:18, Sifra ibid.), he gave strength of spirit to all of Israel. And through his self-sacrifice for Torah study, for even after the government decreed that Torah not be taught he continued to teach Torah in public, he set an example and model for the generations. The Sages said (Berakhot 61b): "When they (the Romans) took Rabbi Akiva out to be executed, it was the time for the recitation of Shema, and they were combing his flesh with iron combs, and he was accepting upon himself the yoke of the kingship of Heaven. His students said to him: Our master, to this extent?! (Surely in a state of such terrible suffering you are exempt from reciting Shema; why do you exert yourself so much to recite it?) He said to them: All my days I was troubled by this verse (Devarim 6:5), 'with all your soul' – even if He takes your soul. I said: When will it come to my hand that I may fulfill it? And now that it has come to my hand, shall I not fulfill it?! He prolonged the word 'eḥad' (One) until his soul departed with 'eḥad.' A heavenly voice went forth and said: Fortunate are you, Rabbi Akiva, that your soul departed with 'eḥad' … A heavenly voice went forth and said: Fortunate are you, Rabbi Akiva, for you are destined for the life of the World to Come."

Israel merited all this through Raḥel, who, although she was of distinguished lineage and the daughter of the wealthiest man in Israel, whereas Rabbi Akiva was the son of converts and an am ha-aretz, loved him and believed in him. In this we learn the great reward of the mitzva of loving the convert, by virtue of which the people of Israel is enriched with sages and righteous people without equal.

Rabbi Meir, too, the student of Rabbi Akiva, was a descendant of Neron, who was a Roman army commander who was about to destroy the Temple, and, realizing that this was a sin, deserted from the Roman army and converted (Gittin 56a). What was special about Rabbi Meir was that he was profound and innovative, "uprooting mountains and grinding them against one another" (Sanhedrin 24a). And the reason the halakha was not established according to him is that, because of his great acuity, his colleagues could not fathom his opinion, and could not establish a system based on it (Eruvin 13b).
